LISTINGS.name: Maya Raghunathan
LISTINGS.tagline: Traditional Mysore-style self practice, six mornings a week, taught one breath at a time.
LISTINGS.philosophy: The posture is not the practice. The practice is what you do on the morning you least want to unroll the mat.
LISTINGS.bio: Maya learned in Mysore over eleven years and now runs a small Mysore room in Indiranagar with no music, no mirrors and a strict 5.30am start. She teaches by hands-on adjustment and by name — the room caps at eighteen so she can watch every breath.

reviews.text: Six months in her Mysore room undid ten years of bad shoulder habits. She corrects almost nothing verbally — she just puts you where you should be.
reviews.author: Arjun T.

reviews.text: Strict, warm, completely unimpressed by how bendy you are. Exactly what I needed.
reviews.author: Freya L.

LISTINGS.name: Daniel Okonjo
LISTINGS.tagline: Slow, musical vinyasa in Hackney — long holds, terrible jokes, no handstand pressure.
LISTINGS.philosophy: I would rather you left the room curious than exhausted. Curiosity brings you back on Thursday.
LISTINGS.bio: Daniel came to yoga late, after a decade of running and a bad knee. He builds classes around one idea a week and returns to it from four directions, so beginners are never guessing what the point was.
LISTINGS.address: The Mill Studio, Chatsworth Road, London E5

reviews.text: First teacher who made me feel like a beginner body was welcome rather than tolerated.
reviews.author: Priya S.

reviews.text: Wonderful Sunday yin. The Tuesday class fills up fast, book early.
reviews.author: Tom H.

LISTINGS.name: Sofia Marchetti
LISTINGS.tagline: Props, precision and patience. Twenty-one years of teaching people with injuries how to stand up straight.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Alignment is not aesthetics. It is the difference between a practice that lasts three years and one that lasts thirty.
LISTINGS.bio: Sofia trained in Pune and has spent two decades working with students recovering from back surgery, hip replacements and long illness. Her classes move slowly and her props cupboard is legendary.

reviews.text: I came after a discectomy, terrified. Two years later I garden again. That is the whole review.
reviews.author: Helena R.

reviews.text: The most technically precise teaching I have found in Europe.
reviews.author: Marc D.

LISTINGS.name: Ananya Bose
LISTINGS.tagline: Prenatal and postnatal practice, live online across four timezones, with a recording every time.
LISTINGS.philosophy: A pregnant body is not a broken body. It is a body doing the single most demanding thing it will ever do.
LISTINGS.bio: Ananya has taught prenatal yoga since 2015 and works closely with two midwifery practices. Every live class is recorded and stays available, because nobody in their third trimester should have to make a 7am start.
LISTINGS.address: Online — Zoom links sent on booking

reviews.text: Did every week of my pregnancy with her and then straight into the postnatal series. She explains the why behind every modification.
reviews.author: Nadia K.

reviews.text: The recordings saved me. I practised at 4am more than once.
reviews.author: Emma C.

LISTINGS.name: Koji Yamada
LISTINGS.tagline: Hard, quiet, unfashionable Ashtanga in Greenpoint. Arrive early, leave without a photograph.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Discipline is a kindness you do for your future self. Nothing about it needs to be joyless.
LISTINGS.bio: Koji has practised the same sequence every morning for sixteen years and teaches it the way it was taught to him: by counting, by adjusting, and by refusing to add anything decorative.

reviews.text: Zero nonsense. He remembered my name and my tight left hip after one visit.
reviews.author: Rachel B.

reviews.text: Genuinely difficult. Come with some mileage already.
reviews.author: Devon P.

LISTINGS.name: Elena Petrova
LISTINGS.tagline: Trauma-informed restorative practice — invitational language, no hands-on, doors stay unlocked.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Choice is the technique. Every instruction I give is an offer you are free to decline, and that is the point.
LISTINGS.bio: Elena trained in trauma-sensitive yoga and works with two Berlin support organisations alongside her public classes. Nothing in her room is mandatory, including keeping your eyes closed.

reviews.text: The first yoga class I have been able to stay in the room for. She means it when she says everything is optional.
reviews.author: Jo K.

reviews.text: Extraordinary care in how she speaks to a room.
reviews.author: Miriam S.

LISTINGS.name: Ravi Deshmukh
LISTINGS.tagline: Classical hatha and philosophy study, taught the long way round, over years rather than weekends.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Asana is one of eight limbs. If you have spent ten years on one limb, you have not been doing yoga. You have been stretching.
LISTINGS.bio: Ravi teaches a small classical hatha group and a weekly Sanskrit and sutra study open to anyone who turns up twice. Terms run in six-month blocks.

reviews.text: The sutra study changed how I think about the whole practice. He asks more questions than he answers.
reviews.author: Meera J.

reviews.text: Old school in the best sense.
reviews.author: Chris W.

LISTINGS.name: Tomás Ferreira
LISTINGS.tagline: Short, well-made online classes for people with thirty minutes and a hallway.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Twenty honest minutes beats an ambitious ninety you never actually do.
LISTINGS.bio: Tomás builds every class to fit a small space and a tight schedule, with a clear plan announced at the start so you know exactly what you have signed up for.

reviews.text: Consistent, unfussy, and the only teacher whose classes I have actually kept up for a year.
reviews.author: Lucia G.

reviews.text: Wish there were more advanced options, but the fundamentals are excellent.
reviews.author: Ben O.

LISTINGS.name: Harriet Cole
LISTINGS.tagline: Strong, sweaty flows and a very good Wednesday prenatal class, both in the same church hall.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Strength and softness are not opposites. Most people arrive over-committed to one of them.
LISTINGS.bio: Harriet has taught in Bristol for a decade and runs a teacher mentoring circle. Her general classes are physically demanding; her prenatal classes are anything but.
LISTINGS.address: St Michael's Hall, Montpelier, Bristol BS6

reviews.text: Monday class is the hardest hour of my week and I would not skip it.
reviews.author: Owen D.

reviews.text: Hall is a bit cold in January. Harriet is not.
reviews.author: Sam L.

LISTINGS.name: Millpond Yoga
LISTINGS.tagline: Two rooms, fourteen teachers and a timetable that runs from 6.30am to 9pm, seven days a week.
LISTINGS.philosophy: A studio should be the least interesting thing in the room. We hire well and then get out of the way.
LISTINGS.bio: Millpond opened in a converted print works in 2014 and now runs around sixty classes a week across two rooms, plus a livestream of the evening slot. Mats, blocks and tea are free; the changing rooms have actual lockers.

reviews.text: The only studio I have joined where the beginner class is taught by the most senior teacher rather than the newest one.
reviews.author: Ruth A.

reviews.text: Busy at 6pm — go earlier or livestream. Otherwise faultless.
reviews.author: Deniz K.

LISTINGS.name: Anahata Shala
LISTINGS.tagline: A traditional shala with a Mysore room, a philosophy library and an Ayurvedic clinic upstairs.
LISTINGS.philosophy: We teach in terms rather than drop-ins because the practice is cumulative and so is the teaching.
LISTINGS.bio: Anahata has run continuously since 2007. The morning Mysore room seats forty, the afternoon is given over to teacher training, and the upstairs clinic runs Ayurvedic consultations twice a week.

reviews.text: Feels like a school rather than a gym. That is either exactly what you want or exactly what you do not.
reviews.author: Kavya R.

reviews.text: The library alone is worth the term fee.
reviews.author: Ian F.

LISTINGS.name: Salt Room Yoga
LISTINGS.tagline: A small sea-facing room in Muizenberg with sunrise flows, evening yin and a Thursday breathwork circle.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Every class here is donation-based on Fridays. Nobody has ever abused that and we are not going to stop.
LISTINGS.bio: Salt Room seats twenty-two, faces the water and opens its doors when the wind allows. Five teachers share a timetable that deliberately leaves the middle of the day empty.

reviews.text: Sunrise over False Bay through the doors. Hard to review objectively.
reviews.author: Sipho N.

reviews.text: Small, friendly, occasionally windy. Book the 6.15.
reviews.author: Anna V.

LISTINGS.name: Ten Days of Silence
LISTINGS.tagline: A genuinely silent ten-day sit above the Ganges. No phones, no reading, no eye contact, no exceptions.
LISTINGS.philosophy: We do not make the retreat comfortable, because comfort is the thing you came here to stop chasing.
LISTINGS.bio: Run twice a year by two teachers who have between them sat over forty long retreats. Twenty places, simple shared rooms, three vegetarian meals, and a daily schedule that starts at 4am. Applications close eight weeks before.

schedule.what: Sitting, walking, one hour of instruction

reviews.text: Days four and five were the hardest thing I have done. Day nine is why people come back.
reviews.author: Peter M.

reviews.text: Do not book this as your first retreat. Do book it eventually.
reviews.author: Saskia B.

LISTINGS.name: Slow Week Algarve
LISTINGS.tagline: Seven days, two classes a day, a swimming pool and absolutely no schedule between eleven and five.
LISTINGS.philosophy: The point of a retreat week is the gap in the middle of the day. We protect it fiercely.
LISTINGS.bio: A restored farmhouse an hour inland from Faro, running eight retreat weeks a year for a maximum of sixteen guests. Morning vinyasa, evening yin, long lunches and a cook who does not believe in small portions.
LISTINGS.address: Quinta do Vale, near Loulé, Faro district

reviews.text: The unstructured afternoons are the whole design. I slept nine hours a night for a week.
reviews.author: Claire T.

reviews.text: Excellent for a first retreat. Nobody is competitive, the food is absurd.
reviews.author: Marco P.

LISTINGS.name: Highland Winter Sit
LISTINGS.tagline: A four-night midwinter retreat in a Highland bothy: cold walks, long sits, wood smoke and early nights.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Winter is not a problem to be solved. Four days of going along with it changes the rest of the season.
LISTINGS.bio: Small and deliberately austere — twelve people, one fire, no wifi. Two facilitators lead morning breathwork, an afternoon walk in silence and an evening sit.

reviews.text: Freezing, beautiful, and the best four days of sleep I have had in years.
reviews.author: Fiona G.

reviews.text: Genuinely no wifi. Plan for that with work.
reviews.author: Alec S.

LISTINGS.name: Leila Haddad
LISTINGS.tagline: Kriya, pranayama and long meditations for people who cannot sit still — she was one of them.
LISTINGS.philosophy: You do not calm the mind by asking it politely. You give it something rhythmic and difficult to do.
LISTINGS.bio: Leila teaches kriya and pranayama with an unusually practical bent, and runs a free Sunday sitting group in the Panier. She works often with people managing anxiety and shift work.

reviews.text: The Thursday breathwork replaced my morning coffee, which I did not expect to type.
reviews.author: Camille F.

reviews.text: Intense first few sessions. Stick with it.
reviews.author: Yanis M.

LISTINGS.name: Yusuf Karim
LISTINGS.tagline: Evening breath and nervous-system work for desk-bound bodies, finishing with a long guided sit.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Most of my students sit for nine hours a day. The practice has to answer that, or it is decoration.
LISTINGS.bio: Yusuf built his teaching around the specific damage of office work — jaw, thoracic spine, shallow breathing — and finishes every session with fifteen minutes of guided sitting.

reviews.text: My neck stopped clicking after two months. I have no other explanation.
reviews.author: Farah A.

reviews.text: Lovely closing meditations, sometimes runs over.
reviews.author: Nick R.

LISTINGS.name: Conor Walsh
LISTINGS.tagline: Live conscious-connected breathwork sessions online, with a facilitator on the call throughout.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Big breathwork can bring things up. Doing it alone from a video is not the same as doing it with someone watching.
LISTINGS.bio: Conor runs small live sessions capped at twelve so he can see every face, plus a gentler weekly downregulation class for people who found the deep work too much the first time.
LISTINGS.address: Online — live sessions only, no recordings

reviews.text: The screening call told me he takes this seriously. So does the session.
reviews.author: Hannah W.

reviews.text: Not a soundtrack-and-vibes class. Come prepared to actually feel something.
reviews.author: Raj P.

LISTINGS.name: Anahata 200hr Foundation
LISTINGS.tagline: A residential 200-hour taught over eight weeks rather than four, with philosophy given equal weight to asana.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Nobody becomes a teacher in a month. We stretch the same syllabus over twice the time and expect you to practise between the modules.
LISTINGS.bio: Run by Anahata Shala's six resident teachers since 2011. Mornings are Mysore practice, afternoons alternate between anatomy, Sanskrit, sutra study and supervised teaching. Sixteen places, shared accommodation on site.

reviews.text: Eight weeks instead of four made all the difference. I actually absorbed the philosophy rather than surviving it.
reviews.author: Nisha D.

reviews.text: Demanding, traditional, and they are honest that not everyone finishes ready to teach.
reviews.author: Lars H.

LISTINGS.name: Millpond 300hr Advanced
LISTINGS.tagline: A part-time 300-hour for working teachers — one weekend a month for a year, with online theory in between.
LISTINGS.philosophy: This is a training for people already teaching badly-attended Tuesday classes, and wanting to teach them better.
LISTINGS.bio: Twelve monthly weekends at Millpond plus fortnightly online theory. Heavy on sequencing, hands-on assisting, and the unglamorous business of holding a regular class. You must be teaching at least once a week to enrol.

reviews.text: The assisting module alone rewrote how I teach. Worth it for that weekend.
reviews.author: Georgia N.

reviews.text: Fitting it around a full-time job was hard but the monthly rhythm makes it possible.
reviews.author: Adam R.

LISTINGS.name: Foundations 200hr Online
LISTINGS.tagline: A fully online 200-hour with live teaching practice in small groups — no pre-recorded lecture dumping.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Online training gets a bad name because most of it is video. Ours is ninety per cent live, in groups of six.
LISTINGS.bio: Twenty-four weeks, two live evenings a week plus a Saturday morning, capped at twenty-four students split into practice pods of six. Recordings exist but attendance is expected. Suits people without a good training within travelling distance.
LISTINGS.address: Online — live sessions, three timezone options

reviews.text: I live four hours from the nearest studio. This was the only realistic option and it turned out to be a good one.
reviews.author: Katrin S.

reviews.text: The pods are the reason it works. You teach to the same five people for six months.
reviews.author: Oli B.

LISTINGS.name: Junko Nakamura
LISTINGS.tagline: Zazen in a temple sub-hall, twice daily, plus a monthly all-day sit open to complete beginners.
LISTINGS.philosophy: There is nothing to attain and nothing to improve. Sit down, face the wall, and let that be disappointing for a while.
LISTINGS.bio: Junko has practised in the Sōtō tradition for twenty-four years and teaches a lay sitting group with no fees and no membership. Beginners are given twenty minutes of posture instruction before their first sit and then left alone.

reviews.text: No ceremony, no explanation, no music. After a month of resenting it I understood.
reviews.author: Tomoko I.

reviews.text: She corrected my posture twice in six months and both times it was the right moment.
reviews.author: Will A.

LISTINGS.name: Dr Ruth Ellis
LISTINGS.tagline: The standard eight-week MBSR course, taught properly, with GP referrals accepted.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Mindfulness is a clinical intervention with an evidence base and real contraindications. I teach it that way, not as a lifestyle.
LISTINGS.bio: Ruth is a clinical psychologist who has taught MBSR since 2010 and supervises other teachers. Courses run three times a year, in person in Chorlton and online, with a full-day silent session in week six.

reviews.text: She was clear at the orientation that this might not be right for me at that point. That honesty is why I came back a year later.
reviews.author: Stephen C.

reviews.text: The silent day is the hinge of the whole course. Do not skip week six.
reviews.author: Amara O.

LISTINGS.name: Priya Nair
LISTINGS.tagline: Yoga nidra and mantra practice, live at 21:00, designed to be done lying in bed with the lights off.
LISTINGS.philosophy: Yoga nidra is not a nap and it is not a sound bath. It is a structured practice, and most people have only ever met a diluted version.
LISTINGS.bio: Priya teaches classical yoga nidra in the Satyananda structure alongside a Sanskrit mantra group. Sessions are live only — she does not release recordings, because people use them as sleep aids and stop practising.
LISTINGS.address: Online — live sessions, GMT and IST

reviews.text: I have used nidra apps for years. Twenty minutes with an actual teacher was a completely different practice.
reviews.author: Jenny F.

reviews.text: Refusing to give out recordings annoyed me at first. She is right.
reviews.author: Dev M.

START_PATHS.note: One thing to read first, then two teachers who will not expect you to know the Sanskrit.

START_PATHS.note: Props, precision, and two teachers used to working around a diagnosis.

START_PATHS.note: Specifically sequenced prenatal practice — not a gentler version of a general class.

START_PATHS.name: I want to sleep better
START_PATHS.note: Downregulating breath and nidra rather than strong flow. Know which kind you are booking.

START_PATHS.note: Meditation taught as its own discipline, from clinical MBSR to traditional zazen.

START_PATHS.note: What separates a good training from a popular one, and two accredited routes.

POSTS.title: The eleven yoga styles, honestly described
POSTS.excerpt: What actually happens in an Ashtanga room versus a yin room, and which one suits the week you are having.
body: Every studio timetable assumes you already know the difference between vinyasa and hatha, between yin and restorative, between a led class and a Mysore room. Almost nobody does. Here is the plain version.

Ashtanga is a fixed sequence, practised in the same order every time. In a Mysore room you do it yourself, from memory, while the teacher moves around the room adjusting people. It is repetitive on purpose: the sequence stops being the thing you are thinking about, and something else becomes available.

Vinyasa borrows Ashtanga's breath-linked movement but throws out the fixed order. A good vinyasa teacher builds towards something; a poor one simply keeps you moving. Ask what the class is working on. If there is an answer, it is probably a good class.

Hatha, in the modern timetable sense, usually means slower, held postures with less flowing between them. Classical hatha is a much larger thing — a whole system that includes breath, cleansing practices and meditation, of which posture is a small part.

Iyengar is precision and props: belts, blocks, chairs, walls. It looks static and is anything but. It is the style most likely to help if you are working around an injury, and the style most likely to tell you your knee is not where you think it is.

Yin holds passive floor postures for three to five minutes to load connective tissue rather than muscle. Restorative looks similar but has the opposite intention — it props you up so completely that nothing loads at all. Yin is uncomfortable. Restorative should not be.

Kundalini uses repetitive movement, breath patterns and sound rather than posture shapes. It is the most polarising style on any timetable and the one people most often either abandon in the first ten minutes or practise for thirty years.

Prenatal is not a gentler version of a general class. It is a differently sequenced practice built around a body whose ligaments, balance and blood volume are all changing month to month. Take the specific class.
The practical advice: try three teachers of one style before you decide the style is not for you. Teachers vary far more than styles do.

POSTS.title: Breathwork is not one thing
POSTS.excerpt: Slow pranayama and conscious connected breathing do opposite things to your nervous system. Know which you booked.
body: The word breathwork now covers two almost opposite practices, and booking the wrong one is the single most common bad experience people have with it.

The first kind is slow and downregulating: extended exhales, gentle retentions, nasal breathing, often taught inside a yoga class as pranayama. The aim is to lower arousal. You should leave calmer than you arrived, and nothing dramatic should happen.

The second kind is fast and activating: conscious connected breathing, holotropic-derived work, sometimes an hour of continuous circular breathing to music. This deliberately shifts blood chemistry and can produce strong physical and emotional responses — tingling, cramping in the hands, tears, occasionally a great deal more.
Neither is better. But a Tuesday-lunchtime slot described only as 'breathwork' could be either, and people book the second expecting the first.

Ask two questions before booking: how long is the active breathing portion, and is a facilitator present for the whole session. Ten minutes with a teacher in the room is a different proposition from fifty minutes with a recording.

If you have a cardiovascular condition, are pregnant, have a history of seizures, or are managing a psychiatric diagnosis, the fast kind needs a conversation with the facilitator first. Good facilitators ask before you do.

POSTS.title: What to expect in your first class, minute by minute
POSTS.excerpt: Nobody will look at you. Here is what happens anyway, so you can stop wondering.
body: Arrive ten minutes early. This is the only rule that matters, and it exists so you can find the mats, the toilets and a spot that is not directly in front of the teacher.
You will be asked whether you have any injuries. Answer honestly and specifically. 'Bad back' is less useful than 'my lower back hurts when I bend forward'.
The first few minutes are usually sitting or lying still. This is the hardest part for most beginners, and it does not stay hard.
You will not know the Sanskrit names. You do not need to. Watch the person next to you for the first two weeks; every single person in the room did the same thing.
Something will be uncomfortable. Sharp, hot or electric means stop. Dull, broad and breathable means stay. Learning that distinction is most of the skill.
The class ends lying on your back for five to ten minutes. Do not leave early. It is not optional padding — it is the part that makes the rest work.
Afterwards you may feel unusually emotional, unusually sleepy, or nothing at all. All three are normal. Drink water and come back on Thursday.

POSTS.title: How to choose a retreat you will actually enjoy
POSTS.excerpt: The three questions that separate a restorative week from an expensive week of feeling trapped.
body: Retreats fail for boringly predictable reasons, and all of them are visible in the schedule before you book.

First question: how much unstructured time is there? A week with two classes a day and a free afternoon is a rest. A week with two classes, a workshop, a talk and a group dinner is a conference with better views.

Second question: how many people? Under sixteen and you will know everyone by day three. Over thirty and you will be in a group that is managed rather than taught. Neither is wrong, but they are completely different weeks.

Third question: is silence involved, and is it optional? Partial silence — mornings only, or meals only — is a very different commitment from ten days of the real thing. Retreats that are vague about this are usually vague in person too.

Two smaller things that matter more than people expect: whether rooms are shared, and how far it is from the airport. A four-hour transfer at the end of a long-haul flight eats the first day and a half.
And book your first retreat close to home. If it turns out not to suit you, a three-hour train back is a very different situation from a rebooked international flight.

POSTS.title: How to tell a good teacher from a popular one
POSTS.excerpt: Follower counts, playlists and photogenic postures measure something. It is not teaching.
body: A popular teacher fills a room. A good teacher notices the person at the back who has been holding their breath for six minutes. These overlap less often than you would hope.

Watch what happens when somebody in the room cannot do the thing. If the teacher offers a genuine alternative — not 'or stay here', but a different shape with the same intention — that is a good sign.

Listen for whether instructions are about shape or about sensation. 'Square your hips' is a shape. 'Find the point where the front of your left hip starts to speak' is a sensation. Good teachers use both and know which one a beginner can actually follow.
Notice whether they teach the same class to everyone. A teacher who has been running the same sequence for three years with a different playlist is not teaching; they are hosting.
Ask how long they have been practising, not how long they have been teaching. The gap between the two numbers is informative.
And notice how you feel two hours later, not two minutes later. Anyone can produce a nice feeling at the end of savasana.

POSTS.title: Buy two blocks before you buy anything else
POSTS.excerpt: A short and slightly grumpy guide to what equipment is worth owning.
body: Two foam blocks. That is the whole shopping list for the first year, and they will do more for your practice than any mat costing more than a modest dinner.

Blocks bring the floor closer. Almost every complaint a beginner has — hamstrings, wrists, lower back in forward folds — is partly a complaint about the floor being further away than their body can currently reach.
A strap is the second purchase, and a dressing-gown cord does the job perfectly until you are certain.
Mats matter less than the internet suggests, with one exception: if you sweat, grip is the only specification that counts. Everything else is thickness preference.
Do not buy a bolster until a teacher has told you to. They are expensive, bulky, and two folded blankets are genuinely as good for the first few years.
Wear something you can be upside down in without adjusting. That is the entire clothing guide.
